category_title: Students who use physical and verbal resistance to negotiate classroom autonomy
minimal_context: The student is participating in a class meeting after lunch to transition to a planned math activity, but wants to continue writing their opinions about race.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Welcome back from lunch and recess. It is time to transition to our planned math activity.

STUDENT: We should keep writing. We can do math tomorrow. Talking about race is important. I might forget what I want to say.

TUTOR: We need to follow the schedule we have set for today.

STUDENT: What if we took turns? So, like, people that want to write can. People who want to do math, can.

TUTOR: We all need to do the same activity right now. Please get ready for math.

STUDENT: Well, I'm going to be super mad if I can't finish my writing. I will just be here and not do anything! (Lies down on the floor)

options.A: Provide the student with access to similar, but more socially appropriate, sensory stimulation, such as a stress ball.
options.B: Be authentic and honest; treat student input as significant and allow it to actually transform pedagogical practice.
options.C: Increase the reinforcer (pay-off) for transitioning to math and decrease the reinforcement for continuing to write.
options.D: Provide the student with an endless supply of math problems to work on during the activity.
